chapters.title: Chapter 6: Liquidity Risk and Liquidity-Adjusted VaR

lessons.title: Liquidity-Adjusted VaR (L-VaR): Building Exit Cost Into the Model

children.text: Liquidity-Adjusted VaR, L-VaR, does exactly what its name says: it takes the standard market risk VaR from Chapter 2 and adds the exit cost from the last lesson directly into the number, producing a single figure that reflects not just how much the market could move against you, but what it would actually cost to get out.

body.label: Liquidity-Adjusted VaR (L-VaR)
body.value: Market risk VaR plus the estimated cost of actually exiting the position
body.context: A standard VaR figure silently assumes this exit cost is zero.

body.caption: The simplest, most widely used form. The liquidity cost term can be built from the participation-based market impact model of the last lesson, or from the spread-volatility model covered below.

children.text: Worked Example: L-VaR for a Sizeable Position
Return to the Rs 1,00,00,000 position in the mid-cap stock from the last lesson, daily volatility 2%, average daily traded value Rs 5,00,00,000, at 99% confidence.

stats.label: Market risk VaR (99%, 1-day)
stats.context: 2.326 x 2% x Rs 1,00,00,000, standard Parametric VaR

stats.label: Liquidity cost
stats.context: Spread plus market impact, from the last lesson's participation-based model

body.text: The liquidity cost adds 21.4% on top of the market risk VaR alone, Rs 99,443 against a base of Rs 4,65,200. A risk report that only shows the Rs 4,65,200 figure has quietly understated this position's true risk by more than a fifth, purely by assuming the exit is free. For a genuinely large or illiquid position, that gap can be even larger.

children.text: A More Rigorous Approach: When Spreads Themselves Widen Under Stress

The participation-based model above captures the cost of your own order overwhelming normal market depth. It says nothing about a separate, equally real risk: the bid-ask spread itself is not a fixed number, it widens during stress, sometimes sharply, even for an order that is not particularly large. Bangia, Diebold, Schuermann, and Stroughair proposed treating the spread itself as a random variable with its own mean and volatility, building a liquidity cost around how wide the spread could plausibly get at a given confidence level, not just how wide it usually is.

body.caption: The Bangia, Diebold, Schuermann, Stroughair (BDSS) approach. Mean spread and spread volatility are both expressed as a percentage of price, z-alpha is the same confidence-level z-score used throughout this course.
BDSS-style liquidity cost for the same position, using stressed spread behavior instead of order-size impact

cells: 0.2% (same as the last lesson's normal-conditions spread)
0.08%, illustrative, spreads can widen meaningfully during stress
0.193% of position value, Rs 19,304 on this Rs 1,00,00,000 position

body.text: Notice this BDSS-style cost, Rs 19,304, is far smaller than the participation model's Rs 99,443 for the same position. That is not a contradiction, the two models answer different questions. The participation model asks what it costs to push a large order through a market of normal depth. BDSS asks what it costs to cross a spread that itself widens under stress, regardless of how large your specific order is. A genuinely large order during a genuinely stressed market faces both effects at once, and a properly built liquidity model needs to combine them carefully without double-counting the spread component both approaches partially capture, a level of precision beyond this course's scope, but the two models here are the right starting building blocks.

body.title: Compute L-VaR Using the BDSS Approach
body.prompt: A Rs 50,00,000 position has a 99% market VaR of Rs 2,32,600. Using the BDSS liquidity cost rate of 0.193% computed in this lesson, what is the total L-VaR, in rupees?

body.title: Choosing the Right Liquidity Model
body.scenario: A risk manager needs to estimate liquidity cost for two very different situations: Situation One, a small Rs 5,00,000 trade in the mid-cap stock during a period of unusually high market-wide stress and volatility. Situation Two, a very large Rs 4,00,00,000 order in the same stock during an otherwise calm, ordinary trading day.
body.prompt: Which liquidity cost model, the participation-based market impact model or the BDSS spread-volatility model, is the better fit for each situation, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Situation One is a better fit for the BDSS spread-volatility model, since the trade itself is small relative to ADV, so order-size impact is minor, but market-wide stress means the spread itself is likely to be unusually wide, exactly the risk BDSS is built to capture. Situation Two is a better fit for the participation-based market impact model, since the order size, 80% of the Rs 5,00,00,000 ADV, is large enough to meaningfully move the price on its own, even though ordinary market conditions mean the spread itself is not unusually wide. Neither model alone captures both situations well, which is exactly why they are complementary tools rather than substitutes for each other.

body.text: A VaR figure without a liquidity cost term is a promise made assuming a frictionless exit. L-VaR is what happens when that promise is honest about the friction, and there is more than one kind of friction to account for.

points: Liquidity-Adjusted VaR adds an estimated exit cost directly onto standard market risk VaR, producing a single figure that reflects the true cost of getting out of a position, not just the risk of holding it.
In the worked example, liquidity cost added 21.4% on top of a Rs 4,65,200 market VaR figure, a gap a standard VaR report would have silently missed.
The participation-based model from the last lesson captures the cost of a large order overwhelming normal market depth, driven by trade size relative to average daily volume.

The BDSS model captures a different risk entirely, the spread itself widening under market-wide stress, relevant even for a normal-sized trade, using the spread's own mean and volatility the same way VaR uses a return's mean and volatility.

These two models are complementary, not interchangeable, a large trade during a calm market and a small trade during a stressed market each call for a different one, and the next lesson pushes further into what happens when both liquidity and stress hit at once.
